text: Setting engineering standards across a team. Leading a postmortem produces a concrete fix for one incident. The next, harder problem is turning a lesson learned once into a standard the whole team actually follows going forward -- and most attempts at this fail not because the standard was wrong, but because of how it was introduced.

A Slack message linking to a new engineering standards document, with no follow-up, is one of the least effective ways to change how a team works. It's not that the content is wrong -- it's that reading a document and changing a habit are different things, and the announcement doesn't close that gap. A standard that isn't discussed, modeled, or checked anywhere quietly fades, especially under time pressure.

There's a sharper distinction underneath that: human-enforced versus tooling-enforced standards. A standard that depends on a reviewer remembering to check for it gets followed inconsistently -- reviewers are busy, tired, or new. A standard enforced by tooling, like a CI check that fails a pull request missing a required section, gets followed consistently, because it doesn't depend on anyone remembering anything. Wherever a standard can be enforced by tooling instead of human vigilance, it should be.

How you introduce a standard matters just as much. A standard delivered as a finished document from the senior engineer tends to be followed resentfully, or not at all -- even a genuinely good one. The more durable approach is to bring the problem to the team first: we've had three incidents now where test data didn't match production, should we have a standard for that? Let the team shape the actual standard, and only then write it down. A standard the team helped design is one the team has ownership of.

And not every standard should be a hard, unbreakable rule. A hard requirement -- every deploy requires an automated test pass -- gets enforced with no exceptions, because the cost of letting it slide is high. A strong default -- prefer this logging library, keep design docs under five pages -- gets followed almost always, but allows a conscious, explained exception. A rigid rule with zero room for judgment tends to produce workarounds and quiet non-compliance instead of real adherence.
Next up: technical debt -- when to pay it down versus ship around it, treating "we should really refactor this" as an actual, computable decision rather than a feeling.
